title: Homily II — The man who seized the bier

edition.locus: Migne, PG 96 (Paris, 1860), Homily II on the Dormition, col. 740 (PDF leaf 411)

source_text: Παρῆσαν δὲ τυχὸν καὶ Ἰουδαῖοι, ὅσοι μὴ λίαν ἀγνώμονες. Οὐχ οἷον δὲ, ὥσπερ ὄψῳ παράρτυμα, τὸ τοῖς πολλῶν περιφερόμενον χείλεσι προσμῖξαι τῷ διηγήματι. Φασὶ γὰρ, ὅτε πρὸς τῇ καταβάσει κατάντους ὄρους γεγόνασιν οἱ τὸ μακάριον σῶμα τῆς Θεομήτορος αἴροντες, Ἑβραῖόν τινα τῆς ἁμαρτίας δοῦλον, καὶ τῆς πλάνης ὑπόσπονδον, τὸν τοῦ Καϊάφα οἰκέτην μιμούμενον, ὃς τὸ Δεσποτικὸν καὶ θεῖον τοῦ Χριστοῦ τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν ἐῤῥάπικε πρόσωπον, καὶ διαβόλου γενόμενον ὄργανον, θρασείᾳ ῥύμῃ καὶ ἀλογίστῳ φερόμενον, καὶ φορᾷ κακοδαίμονι αὐτομολῆσαι πρὸς ἐκεῖνο τὸ θειότατον σκήνωμα, ᾧ δεδιότες προσῄεσαν ἄγγελοι, καὶ ἀμφοῖν τοῦ κραββάτου ταῖν χεροῖν μανικῶς καὶ ἐκφρόνως δραξάμενον καθέλκειν εἰς τοὔδαφος· φθόνου τοῦ ἀρχεκάκου καὶ τοῦτο ὅρμημα, ἀλλ' ὁ καρπὸς τῶν πόνων προέφθασε, καὶ βότρυν πικρὸν καὶ ἐπάξιον τῆς οἰκείας ἐτρύγησε προαιρέσεως. Ἐκλελοιπέναι γὰρ αὐτὸν τὰς χεῖρας διαγορεύουσι. Καὶ ἦν ἰδεῖν τοῦ ἀτόπου τολμήματος τὸν αὐτόχειρα ἀθρόον δεικνύμενον ἄχειρα, ἕως πρὸς πίστιν τὴν γνώμην μετέβαλε, καὶ μετάμελον. Ἀμελητὶ γὰρ οἱ τὸν κράββατον φέροντες ἔστησαν, καὶ ἐπιθεὶς τὼ χεῖρε ὁ δείλαιος τῷ ζωαρχικῷ καὶ θαυμαστοτόκῳ σκηνώματι, σῶος αὖθις ἐκ κολοβόχειρος γίνεται. Ἐπίσταται γὰρ ὡς τὰ πολλὰ καὶ περιστάσεις σῶα καὶ σωτήρια κύειν βουλεύματα. Ἀλλ' ἐπὶ τὸ προκείμενον παλινοστήσωμεν.
pass_a_gloss: There were present (πάρειμι) perhaps (τυχόν) also Jews, as many as [were] not very (λίαν) unfeeling/unreasonable. Not out of place [is it], like a relish to a dish (ὄψον), to mix into the narrative (διήγημα) what is carried about on the lips (χείλη) of many. For they say (φασί) that when those lifting (αἴρω) the blessed body of the God-mother came to the descent of a steep mountain/hill (ὄρος), a certain Hebrew (Ἑβραῖος), slave (δοῦλος) of sin (ἁμαρτία) and treaty-bound to error (πλάνη), imitating the household servant (οἰκέτης) of Caiaphas (Καϊάφας), who slapped (ῥαπίζω) the Master's and divine face of Christ our God, and having become an instrument (ὄργανον) of the devil, borne (φέρομαι) by a bold (θρασεῖα) and unreasoning rush (ῥύμη) and an ill-starred impulse (φορά), deserted/rushed over to that most divine tabernacle (σκήνωμα), which angels approached fearing (δείδω), and with both hands (χεῖρε) madly (μανικῶς) and senselessly grasping the bed/bier, was dragging down (καθέλκω) to the ground (ἔδαφος); of envy (φθόνος) of the evil-originating [one] this too [was] an onrush (ὅρμημα) [R. φθόνῳ]; but the fruit (καρπός) anticipated the labours (πόνοι), and a bitter (πικρός) cluster (βότρυς) and worthy (ἐπάξιος) of his own choice he harvested (τρυγάω). For that his hands had failed (ἐκλείπω) they declare. And it was possible to see the self-handed doer of the outrageous (ἄτοπον) daring (τόλμημα) all at once (ἀθρόον) shown handless (ἄχειρ), until he changed his mind (γνώμη) to faith (πίστις) and regret. For without delay those carrying the bier stood still (ἵστημι), and the wretch (δείλαιος), having laid the two hands on the life-originating and wonder-bearing tabernacle, becomes (γίνομαι) sound (σῶος) again from maimed-handed. For misfortunes too know, for the most part, to conceive/bear (κύω) sound (σῶα) and saving (σωτήρια) counsels. But to the matter at hand let us return home.
pass_b_english: Some Jews too, perhaps, were present, those of them who were not wholly unreasonable. It is not out of place to mix into the story, like a relish added to a dish, what is passed around on many lips. For they say that when those carrying the blessed body of the Mother of God had come to the descent of a steep hill, a certain Hebrew, a slave of sin and a sworn ally of error, imitating the servant of Caiaphas who struck the divine face of the Master, Christ our God (John 18:22), became an instrument of the devil. Carried along by a reckless and senseless rush and an ill-fated impulse, he flung himself at that most divine tabernacle which the angels approached with fear, and seizing the bier with both hands, madly and out of his mind, he tried to drag it to the ground. This assault too came from the envy of the author of evil. But the fruit came before the labour was done, and he gathered a bitter cluster, well deserved by his own intent.

For they relate that his hands failed him. And one could see the man who had set his own hand to that monstrous outrage suddenly shown to have no hands, until he turned his mind to faith and remorse. For those carrying the bier at once stood still, and the wretched man laid his two hands on that tabernacle, the source of life and bearer of wonders, and from being maimed he was made whole again. For even hardships, as a rule, know how to bring forth sound and saving resolves. But let us return to our subject.

choices.note: The man who struck Jesus' face (ῥάπισμα) is the officer of John 18:22 (before Annas; compare Matthew 26:67, where Jesus is struck in Caiaphas's house); the homily calls him "the servant of Caiaphas".
"Slave of sin" may echo John 8:34 or Romans 6:17, 20; stock phrase, uncited.
"A bitter cluster" may echo Deuteronomy 32:32; uncertain, uncited.
Οὐχ οἷον δέ is an unusual idiom; rendered after the PG Latin "ab re vero non est" ("it is not out of place").
ὅσοι μὴ λίαν ἀγνώμονες: ἀγνώμων means unfeeling, ungrateful or unreasonable; rendered "not wholly unreasonable".

ὁ καρπὸς τῶν πόνων προέφθασε: construed with the PG Latin ("fructus labores praecessit"), the fruit got ahead of the labours, that is, he was punished before he could finish; rendered "the fruit came before the labour was done".

φθόνου τοῦ ἀρχεκάκου is ambiguous: "envy, the first cause of evils" or "the envy of the author of evil" (the devil, as the PG Latin "invidiae malorum auctoris" takes it); the second is rendered (compare Wisdom 2:24, uncited).

ἐκλελοιπέναι τὰς χεῖρας ("his hands had failed"); the PG Latin has "orbatum fuisse manibus" ("deprived of his hands"); the Greek wordplay αὐτόχειρ / ἄχειρ ("doer with his own hand" / "handless") and κολοβόχειρ ("with maimed hands") is kept in sense.
Printed Ἀμελητί is read as ἀμελλητί ("at once"); as printed it would mean "carelessly".
ζωαρχικός ("life-originating") rendered "the source of life"; the PG Latin has "vitae principium ... prodigiorumque fons".
The Greek wordplay σῶος / σωτήριος ("sound" / "saving") is kept.

Review kept "his hands failed him" for ἐκλελοιπέναι αὐτὸν τὰς χεῖρας rather than the PG Latin "orbatum fuisse manibus" ("deprived of his hands"), because he later lays his two hands on the bier (ἐπιθεὶς τὼ χεῖρε).
Printed Ἀμελητί and Οὐχ οἷον δέ confirmed on the page image (leaf 411).
